domain: PDF metadata forensics for tamper detection: producer fingerprinting, DocInfo/XMP cross-validation, trailer /ID analysis, date-format fingerprints, PDF/A markers

techniques.name: Producer/Creator fingerprint database (generator vs editor vs online converter)
techniques.how_it_works: Read /Producer and /Creator from DocInfo (PyMuPDF doc.metadata) and classify against a curated string database in three tiers: (1) GENERATORS that produce first-generation documents: 'Microsoft Word' / 'Microsoft® Word for Microsoft 365', 'LibreOffice X.Y', 'Adobe PDF Library' (+Creator 'Adobe InDesign'), 'Acrobat Distiller', 'pdfTeX-1.40.x', 'Skia/PDF m##' (Chrome print-to-PDF), 'macOS Version ... Quartz PDFContext', SAP/Oracle BI/billing-system strings; (2) EDITORS/LIBRARIES that imply post-generation processing: 'Adobe Acrobat Pro/DC', 'iText'/'iTextSharp', 'Apache PDFBox' (used by Stirling-PDF), 'SAMBox' (Sejda's engine), 'pikepdf', 'itext-paulo', 'Aspose.PDF', 'Photoshop' or 'GIMP' or 'Canva' as Creator on an official document; (3) ONLINE CONVERTERS (empirically measured in the Adhatarao–Lauradoux study): 'www.ilovepdf.com', Sejda='Apache FOP Version 2.3' (conversion) or 'SAMBox 1.1.x' (other ops), Smallpdf='3-Heights(TM)' (compression) or 'Microsoft Word for Office 365' (conversion — they run real Word), PDF24='LibreOffice 6.x'/'GPL Ghostscript 9.x', 'PDF Candy', 'lightpdf.com', 'Online2PDF.com', 'Soda PDF Online', 'zonepdf.com', 'Neevia PDFcompress', 'FreePDF.net PDFill', 'pdfaid using ABCpdf'. Score generator=neutral/positive, editor=medium flag on an invoice, converter=medium flag; institutional-billing producer = small trust bonus.
techniques.signal: Catches lazy tampering (most amateur fraud passes through iLovePDF/Sejda/Acrobat and the Producer betrays it) and confirms legitimacy when the producer matches known billing pipelines. Medium strength: strings are trivially spoofable and some legitimate senders genuinely use converters (CLAUDE.md already notes this). FP risk moderate — flag, don't heavily penalize; note online services often mask themselves as LibreOffice/Ghostscript/Word so a 'LibreOffice' producer on a corporate invoice is itself mildly informative.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python: pymupdf (pip) doc.metadata, plus a JSON string database you maintain. Zero system deps, <1 ms, negligible RAM.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02702 (Adhatarao & Lauradoux, 'Robust PDF Files Forensics Using Coding Style' — Table 11 lists measured producer strings of ~25 online services)
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3437880.3460405 (Exploitation and Sanitization of Hidden Data in PDF Files)

techniques.name: Producer append-chain parsing ('; modified using iText…')
techniques.how_it_works: iText/iTextSharp (AGPL versions and derivatives, which power many online editors including parts of iLovePDF) never replace the Producer when modifying a file — they APPEND: e.g. 'Adobe Acrobat 9.4.1; modified using iTextSharp 5.0.5 (c) 1T3XT BVBA'. Split /Producer on ';' and regex for 'modified using', 'edited', 'converted by', version chains. Each appended segment is one documented processing pass; the first segment reveals the original generator, later segments reveal the editing tools in order.
techniques.signal: Very strong, near-zero-FP tamper/processing evidence: the string literally logs the modification chain, and iText's API deliberately makes it hard to remove (only paid licensees can). Catches invoices generated by a real system then round-tripped through an iText-based editor. Editing is not always fraud (a company may stamp/merge legitimately), so treat as high flag on invoices, critical when combined with amount-bearing pages changing.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python string parsing on doc.metadata['producer']. No deps beyond pymupdf. Microseconds.

techniques.name: Creator/Producer coherence-pair validation
techniques.how_it_works: Maintain a table of known-coherent (Creator, Producer) pairs: ('Microsoft Word', 'Microsoft Word...'), ('Writer', 'LibreOffice 7.x'), ('Adobe InDesign CC', 'Adobe PDF Library 15.x'), ('Chromium'/'Mozilla', 'Skia/PDF m##'), ('LaTeX'/'TeX', 'pdfTeX-1.40.x'), ('PScript5.dll', 'Acrobat Distiller'). Flag incoherent pairs: institutional Creator (SAP, 'Oracle BI Publisher', 'PeopleSoft') with a consumer/editor Producer (iLovePDF, PDF24, Acrobat), or design-tool Creators (Canva, PowerPoint, Photoshop, GIMP) on documents claiming to be invoices/attestations — those tools are how fakes get drawn from scratch. Optionally add per-issuer consistency: if you later match a template (Module I), verify the Producer equals the one that issuer normally uses.
techniques.signal: Medium strength. Catches (a) re-export/editing after original generation, (b) from-scratch fabrication in design tools — the case that defeats pure tamper-detection because the file is 'clean'. FP risk: moderate (legitimate archiving/scanning workflows change the pair); keep at medium severity, escalate only in combination.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python lookup table over doc.metadata. Negligible cost.

techniques.name: DocInfo vs XMP cross-validation
techniques.how_it_works: Extract DocInfo (doc.metadata) and the raw XMP packet (doc.get_xml_metadata() in PyMuPDF, or pikepdf.open_metadata()). Compare the mirrored fields after normalization: /CreationDate ↔ xmp:CreateDate, /ModDate ↔ xmp:ModifyDate, /Creator ↔ xmp:CreatorTool, /Producer ↔ pdf:Producer (normalize PDF 'D:YYYYMMDDHHmmSS+HH'mm'' vs XMP ISO-8601 to UTC before comparing). Flags: (1) date mismatch beyond a few seconds → one metadata layer was edited without the other (metadata-spoofing tools and many naive editors only rewrite DocInfo); (2) DocInfo ModDate LATER than xmp:ModifyMetadataDate → file modified by a non-XMP-aware writer after original export; (3) different Producer/CreatorTool between layers → re-processing; (4) empty DocInfo but populated XMP (or vice versa) → selective scrubbing.
techniques.signal: Strong tamper signal with low FP when dates are timezone-normalized and a small tolerance is used — legitimate single-pass exports from Word/Adobe/LibreOffice write both layers consistently. Agreement between layers is also a mild legitimacy confirmation. Known FP: tools that legitimately update only DocInfo (some CLI utilities), so severity=high only for date contradictions, medium for producer/creator divergence.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python: pymupdf for both layers; parse XMP with stdlib xml.etree or regex (avoid python-xmp-toolkit, which needs the exempi system lib). pikepdf (pip, wheels bundle libqpdf) is a robust alternative. <10 ms per doc.

techniques.name: xmpMM lineage analysis (DocumentID / InstanceID / OriginalDocumentID / DerivedFrom / History)
techniques.how_it_works: Parse the xmpMM namespace from the XMP packet: xmpMM:DocumentID is a GUID meant to persist across a document's life; xmpMM:InstanceID is regenerated on every save; xmpMM:OriginalDocumentID survives 'save as'; xmpMM:DerivedFrom names the source document (stRef:documentID/instanceID) when the file was produced by converting another; xmpMM:History is an ordered array of edit events, each with stEvt:action ('saved','converted'), stEvt:softwareAgent (e.g. 'Adobe Acrobat Pro DC 21.x'), stEvt:when (timestamp), stEvt:changed ('/metadata' vs '/content'). Rules: InstanceID != DocumentID → at least one resave after creation; History entries whose softwareAgent differs from the claimed Producer, or whose stEvt:when timestamps postdate /ModDate or contradict CreationDate ordering → edited; DerivedFrom present on a 'native' invoice → it was converted from something else.
techniques.signal: When present (mostly Adobe-toolchain files), this is a literal edit log — strong, detailed evidence including WHICH tool edited and WHEN, and PDFRecon treats History gaps/ID mismatches as indicators. Absence is normal (most non-Adobe tools don't write xmpMM), so never penalize absence. FP low for contradiction rules; note all of it is forgeable by a sophisticated attacker, so it's supporting evidence, not proof.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python XML parsing of the XMP stream extracted via pymupdf. No extra deps. <10 ms.

techniques.name: Missing/stripped-XMP interpretation for professional documents
techniques.how_it_works: Check whether an XMP metadata stream exists at all (doc.get_xml_metadata() empty?) and whether DocInfo is empty. Interpretation matrix: professional origin claimed (bank, utility, government — known from template/content modules) + no XMP and/or empty DocInfo → suspicious, because Word, Adobe tools, InDesign and enterprise billing systems always emit XMP; whereas developer-generated PDFs (ReportLab, FPDF/fpdf2, PDFKit, Puppeteer/Skia) legitimately omit or minimize metadata. Also flag the 'scrub signature': DocInfo present but all values empty strings, or XMP packet present but containing only a bare rdf:RDF skeleton — signs of deliberate metadata removal.
techniques.signal: Weak-to-medium, context-dependent — use only as a score modifier gated on document type/claimed issuer, never standalone (this is exactly where FPs live: plenty of legitimate SaaS invoices are ReportLab/wkhtmltopdf with no XMP). Deliberate stripping on a corporate document is the interesting case: it usually means the original metadata was incriminating.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python via pymupdf. Negligible cost.

techniques.name: Trailer /ID pair analysis (first vs second identifier)
techniques.how_it_works: The trailer /ID is an array of two 16-byte strings. Per ISO 32000, the FIRST is set once at creation (traditionally an MD5 of time+path+size) and must stay permanent; the SECOND is regenerated on every update. Read via PyMuPDF: doc.xref_get_key(-1, 'ID') (xref -1 = trailer). Rules: (a) ID[0] == ID[1] → consistent with a never-updated original export (mild trust signal); (b) ID[0] != ID[1] → the file WAS updated at least once by a spec-respecting writer (medium flag; combine with revision count and producer); (c) /ID entirely missing → fingerprint of minimalist generators (cairo and Skia/Chrome omit it per the coding-style paper) — informative for producer verification, mildly suspicious if metadata claims Word/Adobe which always write /ID; (d) if multiple revisions exist, compare the /ID in each trailer of the /Prev chain — a changed FIRST ID across revisions violates the spec and indicates crude tampering/rebuilding.
techniques.signal: One-way signal: mismatch proves an update happened (could be benign signing/stamping — DocuSign etc. legitimately produce one update), while equality proves nothing because full-rewrite tools (Ghostscript, many converters) mint a fresh equal pair, erasing history. Low FP for the 'mismatch + suspicious producer + >2 revisions' combination; never flag mismatch alone above medium.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python: pymupdf xref_get_key(-1,'ID') plus a raw-bytes scan of earlier trailers for the /Prev chain. <5 ms.

techniques.name: Incremental-update counting with linearization/signature whitelist
techniques.how_it_works: Count document revisions three redundant ways and reconcile: (1) PyMuPDF Document.version_count (= incremental saves + 1); (2) raw-bytes count of %%EOF + startxref occurrences; (3) walk the trailer /Prev chain. Then whitelist benign causes before flagging: a /Linearized dictionary near the file start means 'Fast Web View' files legitimately contain two %%EOF/startxref even when unedited (classic false positive — check whether the second startxref merely points into the linearization structure); one extra revision containing a /Sig object (digital signature or DocuSign stamp) is a normal signing pass. Scoring: 1 revision = clean; 2 with signature = normal; 3+ or 2 without signature on an invoice = suspicious, escalating when the Producer is an editor/converter.
techniques.signal: Strong and cheap: incremental updates are the PDF format's built-in change journal and resist metadata scrubbing (clearing them requires a full rewrite, which itself changes producer/ID fingerprints). The htpbe reference calls xref count 'the forensic lynchpin'. FP risk handled by the linearization and signature whitelists; remaining FP: legitimate workflows that annotate/stamp (delivery notes) — cap severity at high, not critical.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python: pymupdf version_count + re.findall(rb'%%EOF'|rb'startxref') on the raw bytes. <10 ms even for large files.

techniques.name: Revision archaeology: extract prior versions and diff their metadata/text
techniques.how_it_works: When revisions > 1, reconstruct each earlier version by truncating the file bytes at each successive %%EOF offset and reopening the truncated buffer with fitz.open(stream=...) (MuPDF repairs gracefully). Then diff across versions: DocInfo values (did CreationDate/Producer/amount-bearing text change?), page text extracted per version, /Info object number (a NEW /Info object appended in the last revision while the old Info object still exists as a ghost in the body = metadata was rewritten during the edit — recover the ORIGINAL values from the old object via doc.xref_object() on the orphan). This turns 'file was modified' into 'here is exactly what the fraudster changed', e.g. 1025€ → 2025€.
techniques.signal: The strongest evidence in this whole domain when it fires: you literally recover the pre-tampering content and can show the diff to the user. Near-zero FP for content diffs that alter amounts/dates/names; benign diffs (added signature page, stamp) are recognizable. Limitation: only works when the editor used incremental save (Adobe Acrobat does by default; full-rewrite tools destroy history).
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python with pymupdf + byte scanning; the C tool pdfresurrect (apt install pdfresurrect) does the same as a cross-check. CPU: tens of ms per revision; RAM: one extra copy of the file per version — fine on a small box.
sources: https://github.com/pymupdf/PyMuPDF/discussions/3096 (retrieving all versions of an incrementally saved PDF)
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.10546 (Forensic Analysis of Residual Information in Adobe PDF Files)

techniques.name: Date-string micro-format and timezone fingerprinting
techniques.how_it_works: Fingerprint the raw /CreationDate and /ModDate STRINGS, not just their parsed values: (1) format variant — trailing apostrophe D:20230117161128+05'30' (pre-PDF-2.0 style, written by Acrobat/BFO/most Adobe-era tools) vs no trailing apostrophe (ISO 32000-2 style), 'Z' vs explicit offset vs NO timezone at all, missing 'D:' prefix, truncated precision, or outright malformed dates (JHOVE's PDF-HUL-133 class) — each generator writes ONE consistent style, so a date style inconsistent with the claimed Producer (e.g. Producer says pdfTeX but the date lacks pdfTeX's characteristic format) means metadata was hand-edited or spoofed; (2) internal consistency — CreationDate offset differs from ModDate offset → the modification happened on a different machine/timezone; DocInfo offset differs from the XMP date's offset → layers edited separately; (3) jurisdiction plausibility — a French invoice (EDF, Orange…) should carry +01'00' in winter and +02'00' in summer MATCHING the date's DST period; a UK/US/UTC offset on a claimed-French document, or +01'00' on an August date, is a cheap high-value anomaly.
techniques.signal: Medium-strong as a consistency check with low FP (you only flag contradictions, not absolute values). The DST-vs-date check is a neat non-obvious catch for fraudsters who backdate documents. FPs: multinationals generating invoices centrally in another timezone, UTC-configured servers (many SaaS invoices are legitimately +00'00Z') — so gate the jurisdiction rule on 'claimed local French issuer' templates and keep severity medium.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python regex on the raw DocInfo strings (access unparsed values via pikepdf docinfo or PyMuPDF xref_get_key on the /Info object to avoid library normalization). Negligible cost.

techniques.name: pdfaid PDF/A claim validation (claim vs reality)
techniques.how_it_works: Parse pdfaid:part and pdfaid:conformance from XMP (e.g. part=3, conformance='B' → claims PDF/A-3b, the profile required for Factur-X e-invoices). Then verify the claim is plausible with cheap local checks: all fonts embedded (PyMuPDF page.get_fonts() ext/embedded flags), no encryption, no JavaScript (doc.xref count scan for /JS //JavaScript), XMP present and well-formed, no non-conforming annotations. A file that CLAIMS PDF/A but violates basics was either re-processed by a non-conforming tool after generation (the edit broke conformance but kept the stale XMP claim) or had metadata pasted in. Optional full validation: veraPDF CLI, the PDF Association's official open-source validator, run as a subprocess. PDFRecon classifies 'PDF/A violations (when claimed)' as a high-confidence red flag.
techniques.signal: Two-sided: claimed-and-valid PDF/A on an invoice is a meaningful legitimacy bonus (professional archival pipeline); claimed-but-violated is a strong stale-claim tamper indicator with low FP (conforming generators don't emit broken PDF/A; only post-editing does). No claim = neutral. FP risk mainly from your lightweight checker being stricter than the spec — keep the pure-Python checks to unambiguous rules (font embedding, encryption, JS).
techniques.local_feasibility: Claim parsing + basic checks: pure Python (pymupdf). Full validation: veraPDF is local, free, but Java — apt default-jre-headless, ~200-500 MB JVM RAM, 1-3 s/doc; make it an optional deep-scan path on a small box. Everything runs offline.

techniques.name: Factur-X / ZUGFeRD embedded-XML cross-verification (French invoices)
techniques.how_it_works: French/German hybrid e-invoices embed a machine-readable CII XML file (factur-x.xml) inside a PDF/A-3, declared in XMP under the fx: namespace (DocumentType, DocumentFileName, ConformanceLevel). Pipeline: detect the embedded file (PyMuPDF doc.embfile_names()), extract it, validate against the bundled XSD locally (pip package factur-x, xml_check_xsd()), then cross-check the XML's amounts, dates, seller name, SIRET/VAT and IBAN against the values extracted from the PDF's visible text layer. A fraudster who edits the visible text (Photoshop/iLovePDF/Acrobat) almost never updates the embedded XML → any amount/date/IBAN divergence between XML and text layer is near-certain tampering.
techniques.signal: For documents that carry it: the single strongest signal available — valid + consistent Factur-X is a large trust bonus (France's B2B e-invoicing mandate from Sept 2026 makes coverage grow fast), and XML-vs-text divergence is a critical flag with essentially zero FP (allow rounding/format normalization on amounts). Absence is neutral today. Also check XMP fx: declaration present but attachment missing/invalid = re-processing destroyed the invoice payload.
techniques.local_feasibility: pip: factur-x (pulls lxml, PyPDF) + pymupdf for extraction; fully offline (XSDs ship with the package). ~100-300 ms. Optional deeper EN 16931 business-rule validation exists (Mustang, Java) but XSD + cross-check covers the fraud case.

techniques.name: Coding-style structural producer verification (metadata-independent, anti-spoofing)
techniques.how_it_works:
Fingerprint the generator from the file's raw STRUCTURE and check it agrees with the claimed /Producer — defeats metadata spoofing because structure survives metadata edits. Concrete rules from the Adhatarao–Lauradoux study (192 regex/YARA rules, 11 producers, 74% overall / >90% for LibreOffice, pdfTeX, Word, Distiller, Quartz): (1) header line-2 binary magic: 0xB5B5B5B5=Word, 0xE2E3CFD3=Acrobat Distiller, 0xD0D4C5D8=pdfTeX/LuaTeX(TeXLive), 0xC7EC8FA2=Ghostscript, 0xC3A4C3BCC3B6C39F ('äüöß' UTF-8)=LibreOffice, 0xD3EBE9E1=Skia/Chrome, 0xB5EDAEFB=cairo; (2) trailer key sets: /DocChecksum appears ONLY in LibreOffice trailers; Word uniquely writes TWO trailer objects with /XRefStm; Distiller uses xref streams with /DecodeParms /Columns /Predictor; cairo and Skia omit /ID entirely; (3) object formatting style (key order, whitespace/newline conventions inside dictionaries, e.g. Word objects match /4 0 obj
<</Filter/FlateDecode/Length \d+>>
stream
/); (4) xref table presence/absence. Rule: metadata claims Word but no 0xB5B5B5B5 header, no /XRefStm, wrong object style → Producer string is fake or the file was rebuilt by another tool.
techniques.signal: Strong anti-spoofing signal: a producer/structure CONTRADICTION is highly suspicious with low FP if you only fire on well-attested producers (Word, LibreOffice, pdfTeX, Distiller, Chrome). Match = legitimacy confirmation of the claimed toolchain. FP risk: producer version drift changes styles over time and post-processing legitimately rewrites structure — so score 'mismatch' as medium-high, 'match' as bonus, and 'unknown structure' as neutral; start with ~10 header/trailer rules before investing in object-level rules.
techniques.local_feasibility: Pure Python re module over raw bytes (read first/last few KB of file); optionally pip yara-python for the full ruleset. Milliseconds, no system deps.
sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02702 (full paper: header magic Table 2, trailer keys Table 3, per-tool accuracy Tables 6-10)

techniques.name: Acrobat edit-residue byte-scan (TouchUp_TextEdit and friends)
techniques.how_it_works: Scan the raw file bytes for residue that Adobe Acrobat's text-editing tools leave behind: '/TouchUp_TextEdit' marked-content/PieceInfo entries (written when text is edited with Acrobat's TouchUp/Edit-Text tool), plus related PieceInfo private data ('/PieceInfo', '/ADBE_CompoundType'), and combine with the incremental-update check (Acrobat edits save incrementally by default, so TouchUp residue usually co-occurs with revisions>1). PDFRecon — an open-source Python/PyMuPDF forensic tool built for exactly this use case — classifies TouchUp_TextEdit as a high-confidence 'altered' red flag; its 40+ indicator list (multiple startxref, dangling objects, white overlay rectangles, invisible text, XMP history gaps, ID mismatches) is a ready-made checklist to mine for TrustyFile modules.
techniques.signal: High confidence that TEXT was edited in Acrobat after generation — on an invoice this is precisely the 'change 1025€ to 2025€' scenario. FP very low for the marker itself (it only appears after Acrobat text edits); residual risk is benign edits (fixing a typo before sending), so pair with WHERE the edit sits (amount/date regions → critical).
techniques.local_feasibility: Trivial pure-Python bytes.find on the raw file; PDFRecon itself is Python+PyMuPDF (source on GitHub) and can be mined for rules. Microseconds.

key_insights: Metadata is a claim, not proof: every DocInfo/XMP field is trivially editable, so the highest-value checks are INTERNAL CONSISTENCY cross-checks (DocInfo vs XMP vs raw structure vs date-string style vs trailer IDs) rather than absolute values — a sophisticated forger must keep ~6 independent layers coherent, and almost none do.

Most strong indicators are ONE-WAY: /ID pair mismatch, incremental updates, '; modified using iText', TouchUp_TextEdit prove processing/editing happened, but their ABSENCE proves nothing — full-rewrite tools (Ghostscript, most converters) legally erase all history. Score asymmetrically: presence = flag, absence = neutral.

The biggest blind spot of metadata forensics is from-scratch fabrication: a fake invoice typed in Word/Canva has pristine, consistent metadata. The counters are Creator-class checks (Canva/PowerPoint/Photoshop creator on an 'official' doc), coding-style vs claimed-issuer verification, and TrustyFile's template/content modules — metadata alone cannot carry this case.

Two mandatory false-positive whitelists before flagging revisions: linearized ('Fast Web View') PDFs legitimately contain two %%EOF/startxref pairs when unedited, and a single signing pass (DocuSign, eIDAS signatures) legitimately adds one incremental revision.

The Adhatarao–Lauradoux measurements show online converters usually don't say who they are: Smallpdf shows up as 'Microsoft Word for Office 365' or '3-Heights(TM)', PDF24 as 'LibreOffice'/'Ghostscript', Sejda as 'Apache FOP'/'SAMBox' — so a producer database must map engine strings to services, and 'LibreOffice' on a corporate invoice deserves mild suspicion on its own.

For the French market, Factur-X is the emerging killer feature: the embedded CII XML is a tamper-evident second copy of every amount/date/SIRET — text-layer vs XML divergence is near-zero-FP proof of tampering, and validity is the strongest positive trust signal available; France's 2026 e-invoicing mandate makes coverage grow rapidly.

Everything researched here runs fully locally in pure Python (pymupdf + pikepdf + factur-x + stdlib regex/xml) in well under a second per document; the only heavyweight optional dependency is veraPDF (Java) for full PDF/A validation, and pdfresurrect (apt) as a cross-check for revision extraction.

Revision archaeology (truncate at each %%EOF, reopen with fitz, diff text/metadata across versions) upgrades the verdict from 'file was modified' to 'here is the original amount before the edit' — the single most persuasive output a fraud-detection UI can show, and it is ~50 lines of pure Python.

Scoring should fire on PATTERN COMBINATIONS, not single fields (e.g. years-old CreationDate + institutional Creator + iLovePDF Producer + 3 revisions = high risk; the same converter producer alone = low), which aligns with TrustyFile's existing minimize-false-positives philosophy.
